I've been working this same land in Quzhou for decades. My father farmed here before me, and I know this soil the way I know my own hands. Four point one mu sounds small to outsiders, but it feeds us and keeps us going.

**My thinking:**

For wheat, I plant every October after I finish harvesting the maize. I always use the improved variety — Jimai 22 has done well for me these past several years, better than the old seeds. I rotary-till after maize because the straw needs working in. I apply compound fertilizer at planting and then push urea at jointing stage. My neighbor across the road uses less nitrogen than me, but his yields show it. I water four times: at sowing if the soil is dry, then at jointing, at heading, and again at grain fill. Three people in my house depend on this. I also spray herbicide in winter and hit it with fungicide and insecticide around heading time — the rust comes if you don't watch it.

For summer maize, I plant straight into the wheat stubble right after the June harvest — no time to lose, the season is short. I use Zhengdan 958, it's reliable. I do no-till now since the government promoted it and it saves me time and my back isn't what it used to be. Summer rains help, so I only irrigate twice — once when I plant to ensure germination, once if it's dry at tasseling. I put down fertilizer twice: compound at planting, then chase with urea at jointing. Maize gets an insecticide spray for borers and a herbicide pass early on.

My yields aren't record-breaking but they're steady. Fifty years teaches you steady.
